title: Imam bayildi
subtitle: Aubergines stuffed and braised with tomatoes and onion
excerpt: Imam bayildi are whole aubergines slit and filled with a sweet, slow-cooked onion and tomato mixture, then braised in olive oil until completely tender. The dish is served at room temperature and needs nothing alongside it except bread.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Imam bayildi described as one of the great vegetable dishes of the Ottoman table, with notes on the name and cooking method. Paula Wolfert, The Cooking of the Eastern Mediterranean (1994). The role of generous olive oil in braising the aubergines discussed.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before. Imam bayildi is better at room temperature or lightly chilled than served piping hot.

content.text: Imam bayildi are whole aubergines, slit down the middle, filled with a slow-cooked mixture of onion, tomato, garlic, and olive oil, then braised in more olive oil until the flesh is completely soft and yielding. The filling collapses into the aubergine as it cooks and the whole thing becomes one sweet, silky, deeply savoury thing. Serve at room temperature with bread; it is one of the great Turkish meze dishes.
Peel {{aubergine}} in alternating strips (so the outside looks striped) and make a deep slit lengthways down each one, cutting to within 1 cm of each end. Do not cut all the way through.
Heat half the {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} in a wide pan over a medium-high heat and brown the aubergines on all sides, about five minutes total. They will not be cooked through. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, add the remaining {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} and cook {{onion}} over a medium-low heat for 20 minutes until very soft and golden. Add {{garlic}} and cook for two minutes.

Add {{tomato}}, {{caster-sugar}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Cook for ten minutes until the tomatoes have collapsed into a thick, saucy mixture. Stir in {{parsley-flat}}. Taste and adjust seasoning.

Lay the browned aubergines in a wide, shallow pan or baking dish, slit side up. Ease the slits open gently and spoon the filling generously into each one, pushing it deep into the cavity. Heap any remaining filling on top.

Add 150 ml of water to the pan around the aubergines. Cover tightly with a lid or foil and braise over the lowest possible heat for 40 to 45 minutes until the aubergines are completely tender when pierced.
Remove from the heat and leave to cool to room temperature. Squeeze lemon juice from {{lemon}} over the top before serving.

items.symptom: The aubergines are still firm after 45 minutes
items.cause: Pan not hot enough during the braise or not enough liquid
items.fix: Add another 50 ml of water and raise the heat to a low simmer. Check the liquid level every fifteen minutes.

items.symptom: The filling oozes out of the slit during cooking
items.cause: Slit cut too wide or filling overpacked
items.fix: This is normal. The excess filling cooks in the pan and becomes part of the sauce. Spoon it back over at serving.

items.symptom: The filling is sweet but the dish lacks depth
items.fix: Twenty minutes for the onions is the minimum. They should be golden and very soft before the tomatoes are added.

items.symptom: The dish tastes of oil but not much else
items.fix: Season the filling assertively at the tomato stage. Both the filling and the whole braised dish should be well salted.

content.text: Imam bayildi means 'the imam fainted' in Turkish, though the reason is debated. Some say he fainted with pleasure at the dish; others that he fainted at the amount of olive oil used. The dish is one of the most famous Turkish meze and belongs to the Ottoman tradition of zeytinyagli (olive oil dishes), cooked in large amounts of oil and served cold or at room temperature. It is a summer dish in Turkey when aubergines are at their best, but it is made year-round. Greek versions are almost the same.
